vignette:
Mateo speaks of his old life as if describing a different man, a distant relative he once admired. For forty years, he was the unofficial heart of his neighborhood. A community organizer by trade and by nature, he was a man built of solid presence and easy laughter, the kind of person who could coax volunteers for a new community garden with a shared joke and a promise of cold drinks. His hands, thick and calloused, were always building something—a stage for the annual cultural festival, raised garden beds for the elders, a new bench for the park. He was, in his own words, “the guy who held the ladder steady for everyone else.”

That all changed two years ago, on a bright Saturday afternoon. The community was building a small pavilion, and Mateo, then 61, was on the scaffolding, securing a roof beam. He remembers the specific details with a chilling, cinematic clarity: the warm sun on his back, the smell of fresh-cut pine, the sound of neighborhood kids playing nearby. Then came the sharp crack, a sound he describes as “a bone breaking inside the wood.” The world tilted violently. For a split second, there was only a sense of profound surprise, a weightless disbelief, followed by the sickening rush of air and the chorus of panicked shouts from below. He landed on a pile of lumber and dirt. The impact wasn’t just a collision; it was an explosion of pain that seemed to shatter the world from the inside out.

He spent weeks in the hospital and months in rehabilitation, his body a map of surgical scars and aching joints. The community rallied, bringing food and offering help, but Mateo found himself unable to accept it. The man who organized everything couldn’t stand being the project. When he finally came home, the physical pain was a constant, dull roar, but it was the other changes that dismantled his life.

He began to experience the fall over and over. He’d be standing in the kitchen, and the floor will suddenly feel like it’s dropped out from under him, a phantom lurch in his gut that sends him grabbing for the counter, his heart hammering against his ribs. The sound of a truck dropping its tailgate down the street can make him flinch so hard he spills his coffee. He stopped using the step stool to change a lightbulb, preferring to sit in the dim light. Sleep offers no escape; he’s haunted by recurring nightmares of falling from impossible heights, waking up tangled in his sheets, slick with sweat.

The man who lived for connection began to crave isolation. The phone will ring, a familiar number from the neighborhood council, and he’ll just stare at it until it stops. The thought of planning the summer festival, a job that once brought him immense joy, now fills him with a cold dread. All he can see are the potential dangers—a faulty wire, an unstable table, a child tripping. His world, once a place of possibility, has shrunk to a landscape of imminent threats.

His wife, Leilani, tried to reach him, but he says it was like trying to hold onto smoke. His easy-going nature had been replaced by a short-fused irritability. He would snap at her for the smallest things, then retreat into a stony, impenetrable silence. He felt a profound sense of shame, a belief that he was no longer a provider or a pillar of strength, but a fragile burden. “She married a rock,” he says, his voice quiet, “and ended up with a pile of gravel.” She left a year ago.

Now, Mateo spends most of his days in the armchair by his front window. He watches the neighborhood he built carry on without him. He sees neighbors tending to the community garden, their laughter carrying on the breeze. He watches them set up for the very festivals he once orchestrated. He is a ghost in his own life, a spectator to the community that was once his entire world, forever tethered to the moment the ground gave way.
